title: Synthetic heartbeat divergence investigation (wip)
content:
Summary:

Short: Over the past two weeks we observed multiple incidents where synthetic heartbeat checks reported healthy while several customer-facing SLOs were burning. This doc records the investigation, hypotheses, quick mitigations, and proposed runbook/runbook changes to avoid future silent divergence between synthetic monitors and real-user signals. Work in progress.

Impact observed:
- 2024-10-28: SLO burn window for inference-latency-high on us-west1 (p90 latency spikes) but no synthetic heartbeat failures for the same region.
- Customers reported degradation via support channels before any heartbeat-based alert was raised.
- Pager load decreased for these incidents because heartbeats suppressed escalation, delaying operator awareness.

Why this matters:
- Our synthetic checks are used as part of the escalation gating logic in several alert routes (we suppress noisy alerts when heartbeats are down). If the synthetic check is false-positive healthy while real traffic is degraded, suppression hides real problems.

Initial hypotheses (ranked):
1) Coverage mismatch: synthetic heartbeats exercise a small subset of endpoints/paths and use truncated payload shapes; regressions affecting specific model-serving paths were not covered.
2) Aggregator sampling bias: synthetic tests run at fixed intervals that miss short-lived but repeated bursts (burstiness on real traffic).
3) Metric instrumentation gap: some downstream dependency (kv-cache, scheduler) emits metrics under a different label set; synthetic check uses a label-normalized path so the alert query omitted the broken series.
4) Alert routing bug: heartbeat signal was being read from a stale Prometheus replica with delayed scrapes due to network partition (less likely given timeline).

Investigation timeline (notes):
- 2024-10-28 09:12: Incoming customer report: 30% error rate on /v1/generate for tenant-42. Support paged SRE.
- 09:15: Check synthetic heartbeats: all green across us-west1; synthetic p99 latency 120ms.
- 09:20: PromQL queries run on live cluster show p95 latency spike (see queries below).
- 09:32: Confirmed mismatch: synthetic test used model-id=redwood-mini and path=/v1/generate?simple=true; customer traffic used model-id=redwood-2B-latency-optimized and large payloads.
- 10:00: Instrumentation audit: found a missing label mapping on gpu-scheduler_exporter that prevented the per-model latency metric from being recorded under model_id for particular pods.

What we ran (commands / queries):
- PromQL to compare synthetic vs real request counts:
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="synthetic-checker"}[1m])) by (region) 
  vs
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="gateway", route=~"/v1/generate.*"}[1m])) by (region)
- PromQL to find latent series mismatch:
  count by (model_id)(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="gateway", le="0.5"})
- kubectl to check pods in us-west1 serving pool:
  kubectl get pods -n inference-us-west1 -o wide --selector=service=model-serving
- Quick grep of exporter config to check label rewriting rules:
  git grep -n "model_id" observability/exports || true

Immediate mitigations applied (short term):
- Disabled heartbeat-based alert suppression for the routes that map to multi-model gateway (rolled out at 10:45). Rationale: keep real-traffic alerts visible until coverage improved.
- Added emergency temporary alert: high p95 latency for route=/v1/generate OR model_id=~".*" with short evaluation window (2m) to capture bursts (10:55).
- Re-ran synthetic check configuration to add a second test path that hits the multi-model gateway with a wide-payload shape (11:20).
- Notified support and oncall teams via Slack thread #sre-incident-512.

Root cause (current working conclusion):
- Primary: synthetic monitoring did not exercise the multi-model gateway or the large-payload codepath. A label-mapping bug in an exporter masked per-model latency series for affected pods, so alert rules that depend on that label did not evaluate the degraded series.
- Secondary: gating logic that suppresses alerts based on heartbeat status created a blind spot.

Runbook changes proposed (short and medium term):
- Short term (must ship in 1 sprint):
  - Expand synthetic monitoring matrix: add tests for N=3 representative models per region, including a heavy-payload test and a model that exercises KV-cache behavior. (owner: Priya)
  - Create a PromQL parity check job that compares synthetic vs real p95/p99 deltas per region and surfaces when delta > 2x for 5m. (owner: Daniel)
  - Remove heartbeat-based suppression from any alert rule that is used for customer-facing SLOs until parity checks exist. (owner: SRE rotation)
  - Add checklist item in oncall runbook: "if SLO burn reported by customers but heartbeat is green, run parity queries (sample provided below)".
- Medium term (1–2 quarters):
  - Build synthetic-to-routing map: canonical mapping of synthetic check -> routes -> model_ids -> pods. Use this to automatically flag coverage gaps. (owner: Observability eng)
  - Add exporter integration tests in CI to validate label rewriting logic after config changes. (owner: platform eng)

Updated runbook snippet (to insert into oncall guide):
1) Initial intake: confirm customer impact and time window.
2) Compare synthetic vs real request counts and latency:
   - Query A (synthetic): sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="synthetic-checker"}[5m])) by (region)
   - Query B (real): sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="gateway", route=~"/v1/generate.*"}[5m])) by (region)
   - If B > A*3 or latency(B p95) > latency(A p95)*2 -> escalate immediately and disable suppression for relevant routes.
3) Check exporter labelsets:
   - count by (model_id)(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="gateway"}) should show the same model_id cardinality as the list in infra-config/model-deployment.yaml.
4) If missing series, remediate by restarting exporter or rolling forward the config as follows:
   - kubectl rollout restart daemonset/gpu-scheduler-exporter -n observability
   - re-run PromQL above after 30s; if still missing, escalate to platform eng.

Pager steps for immediate awake-on-call (if SLO burn but synthetic green):
- Step 0: Acknowledge ticket and post to #sre-incident-512.
- Step 1: Run parity queries (copy above).
- Step 2: Reproduce the failing path with a cURL that mirrors customer payload if possible. Example:
  curl -X POST https://gateway.us-west1.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '@heavy-payload.json' -v
- Step 3: If reproduction shows degradation, remove heartbeat suppression for the route and create a short-lived high-sensitivity alert.

Open action items (owners and due dates):
- Priya: add heavy-payload synthetic test matrix and deploy by 2024-11-18.
- Daniel: implement parity-check PromQL job and dashboard by 2024-11-25.
- Platform: audit exporter label rewrite rules and add CI checks by 2025-01-15.
- SRE: update oncall runbook with the snippet above by 2024-11-10 (in progress).

Lessons and notes for future incidents:
- Synthetic monitors must be treated as a canary for routing surfaces, not as the single source of truth. We need automated parity checks.
- Suppression logic is useful but dangerous when synthetic coverage is narrow; prefer suppression only when synthetic matrix covers the affected route and model mapping.
- Add a short test harness for runbook commands so the oncall can execute a reproduce curl from a secure notebook with preloaded tokens (to avoid copy-paste mistakes).

Appendix: troubleshooting quick commands (copyable)
- List exporter series cardinality by label:
  curl -g 'https://prometheus-query/api/v1/query?query=count by (model_id)(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="gateway"})' | jq '.'
- Example PromQL parity alert (prototype):
  abs((real_p95 - synth_p95) / max(real_p95, synth_p95)) > 0.5 for 5m

Notes: will iterate on wording and add graphs (screenshot exports) to Confluence page. This doc will be used as the working source for the post-incident runbook edits.

-- Ava
